newsitem.title: GERMANY: Broker sees balanced nickel markets in 1997, 1998.
newsitem.headline: Broker sees balanced nickel markets in 1997, 1998.

text.p: The nickel market in 1997 should see a small deficit of 4,000 tonnes in 1997 compared with a 4,000 tonne surplus in 1996, said Helen Williamson, research analyst with London brokers Brandeis Ltd.
In 1998, the market should be even more balanced, in deficit by just 1,000 tonnes.

Speaking at the Metal Bulletin stainless steel conference, she said, "This balanced market (in the next two years) will be reflected in a levelling off of total nickel stocks around 195,000 tonnes compared to 199,000 in 1996."
"As a result, we forecast a steady but modest improvement in prices compared to 1996."

Brandeis currently pegged the three-month nickel price on the London Metal Exchange (LME) at $7,500-8,000 a tonne for the rest of this year, reaching lows in the third quarter before recovering in the fourth.
Williamson said prices in the first half of 1997 had been disappointing, albeit above those in 1996.
Nickel prices in Jan-June averaged $7,585 compared with the 1996 full year average of $7,612.
They were at $7,040/7,050 in late LME dealings on Wednesday.
Strike action at Inco's Sudbury, Ontario, division could push prices to $8,000 but a lengthy labour dispute at Inco has not occurred since 1978-79.
Brandeis was also keeping an eye on developments at the Falconbridge Ltd group's Sudbury operations, where the current labour contract expires at the end of August.
Elsewhere, bearish news was weighing on initially higher price forecasts.
LME stocks of 52,728 tonnes were last at three-and-a-half weeks of consumption, having risen by 21,000 tonnes from July 1996 lows.
Stainless steel output was forecast to grow this year, but finished product stocks across the globe were above historical averages.
Mills might cut output in the second half of 1997.
With two thirds of nickel demand derived from stainless uses, this implied lower demand for nickel.

Other unknowns were possible disruptions to the supply of Russian material or to the currently abundant suppply of nickel scrap, unexpected Cuban and Chinese nickel exports and possible labour problems at smelters in New Caledonia.
